## Guided Tutorial 10.1: Joining the Variance to Its Work Orders and Products

**Context and objective.** The WorkOrderClose table records each variance but not the product that produced it. In this tutorial, you will join the closes to their work orders and items, test that every close finds its match, and summarize the variance by item group and year. You will also check the total against the ledger and rank the items that carry the most variance.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Chapter 9, and open CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite in DB Browser for SQLite on the **Execute SQL** tab. Start a new script for the chapter, with a header comment like the one in Tutorial 9.3, and save it as `Chapter10.sql`.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Join the closes to their work orders.** Each close carries the WorkOrderID of the work order it closes.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, wo.WorkOrderNumber,
       wo.ItemID, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID;
   ```

b. Read the number of rows in the message pane.
c. Run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM WorkOrderClose;` and compare the two numbers.

The join returns exactly as many rows as the WorkOrderClose table holds, many thousands. Every close therefore matches one work order, and none has been dropped by the inner join.

**Step 2. Add the items.** The work order's ItemID leads to the Item table.

a. Add a second join and the item's columns, so that the query reads as below, and run it.

   ```sql
   SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, i.ItemCode,
       i.ItemName, i.ItemGroup, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID;
   ```

b. Confirm that the number of rows is unchanged.

Each close now carries the code, name, and group of the item its work order made. The row count is the same as in Step 1, so every work order matches an item.

**Step 3. Total the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group, and check it against the ledger.** A summary is only useful if it agrees with the books.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT i.ItemGroup, COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   WHERE woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY i.ItemGroup
   ORDER BY TotalVariance DESC;
   ```

b. Run the query below, which totals the variance postings of fiscal 2026 in the ledger that Tutorial 9.2 isolated.

   ```sql
   SELECT ROUND(SUM(gl.Debit) - SUM(gl.Credit), 2) AS LedgerVariance
   FROM GLEntry AS gl
   WHERE gl.AccountID = 93 AND gl.FiscalYear = 2026
       AND gl.SourceDocumentType = 'WorkOrderClose';
   ```

c. Add up the TotalVariance column of item a and compare it with the ledger total.

Three item groups carry the variance: Furniture, Lighting, and Textiles, the groups whose items Charles River makes. Furniture holds more than two-thirds of it. The three groups add up to the ledger total to the cent, so the work order records and the ledger tell the same story.

**Step 4. Compare the three years.** The year of a close is the first four characters of its CloseDate.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT i.ItemGroup, SUBSTR(woc.CloseDate, 1, 4) AS CloseYear,
       COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.OverheadVarianceAmount), 2) AS OverheadVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   GROUP BY i.ItemGroup, CloseYear
   ORDER BY i.ItemGroup, CloseYear;
   ```

b. For each item group, compare the three years of TotalVariance and of Closes.

The result, shown in @fig-10-03, holds one row for each group and year. Furniture's variance rose in each year, to nearly twice its fiscal 2024 level, and Lighting's rose too, while Textiles rose and then fell back. In every group, the number of closes fell over the same period, so a larger variance was spread over fewer work orders. The overhead part moves with the total in each group.

![The Manufacturing Variance by Item Group and Year.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-03-variance-by-group-year.svg){#fig-10-03 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL tab. The query joins WorkOrderClose to WorkOrder and Item and groups the closes by item group and close year, with the number of closes, the total variance, and the overhead variance. The result holds nine rows, three years each for Furniture, Lighting, and Textiles. The Furniture rows, whose total variance rises in each year while the number of closes falls, are outlined."}

**Step 5. Rank the items.** Group by the item's key, and include its code and name so that the result is readable.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT i.ItemID, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName, COUNT(*) AS Closes,
       ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance
   FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
       INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
       INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
   WHERE woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
   GROUP BY i.ItemID, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName
   ORDER BY TotalVariance DESC
   LIMIT 10;
   ```

b. Read the items and their totals, and note the item groups they come from.

The largest totals of fiscal 2026 belong to a mix of dining tables, sideboards, and a throw blanket, each with a few dozen closes. No single item stands out: the variance is spread across most of the items Charles River makes, which points to a cause that affects production as a whole rather than one product.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the joins in Steps 1 and 2 return as many rows as the WorkOrderClose table holds;
- the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group adds up to the ledger total of Step 3;
- Furniture carries most of the variance, and its variance rose in each year while its number of closes fell;
- the ten largest items are spread across several product types.

The variance is not a product problem. It rises across the groups the plant makes, while the number of work orders falls, and that pattern turns the question toward the cost of production itself.
